segments.text: Logic, level two. After logging in as level2, the first question is what the challenge actually is. The /levels/level2 directory holds the classic stack challenge source and a handful of player-recompiled binaries - but note: the real setuid level2 binary is gone. The only level3-readable thing left is level2.c and a small file called level2_alt.

Listing it: a dot-sh, an exploit dot py, getenv, a small c file, level2 itself, level22, level2_alt, set, and shellcode. The dates tell the story - level2 dot c from twenty-ten and level2_alt from twenty-fourteen are the originals; everything else is players' debris from later years.

Reading level2 dot c confirms it: a classic strcpy overflow with the password blanked out to X's, and the source header says password blanked, enjoy. The setuid binary that shipped with this source no longer exists on the box, so that path is dead.

That leaves level2_alt - two hundred and one bytes, readable by level3 only, so clearly the intended target. It carries a Julius Caesar quote: as a rule, men worry more about what they can't see than about what they can. Below it, the ciphertext: B P M X I A A E W Z L G W C I Z M T W W S Q V O N W Z Q A X Q H Q X U E S M K. A Caesar quote next to uppercase ciphertext is a hint, not a flourish: try every Caesar shift.

We write the decoder in vi - and there's a portability gotcha here: the box runs Python two point four, which rejects conditional expressions, so the shift logic uses explicit if-else inside the loop. For each shift one through twenty-five, walk the ciphertext, rotate letters by minus k around their case's base, and print shift and plaintext.
Save it - fifteen lines, three hundred ninety-nine bytes - and run it. Twenty-five candidate plaintexts scroll past.

Shift eight is the one: T H E P A S S W O R D Y O U A R E L O O K I N G F O R I S P I Z I P M W K E C. The password you are looking for is P I Z I P M W K E C. Fun detail: shift twelve accidentally reads LEVELISGAY - the intended level-2-to-level-3 gap message.

One more gotcha before we use it: this box cannot reach its own SSH daemon from inside, so we exit to the client terminal and open the level3 session from there. Level3's ancient sshd is pickier than level2's - it rejects the HostKeyAlgorithms and KexAlgorithms options entirely, so this connection drops them and keeps only StrictHostKeyChecking.

We land with u i d six-zero-two, level3, in the nosu group, and tilde slash dot pass confirms: P I Z I P M W K E C. Level two solved - not with a buffer overflow, but with a two-thousand-year-old cipher the box literally handed us the hint for.
